newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Analyst warns of Argentine harvest bottlenecks.
newsitem.headline: Analyst warns of Argentine harvest bottlenecks.

text.p: Argentina's agricultural output is growing faster than the infrastructure it needs to store it and move it to port, a private analyst warned.

While a dry spell in the northern stretches of the grain belt may yet mean that the harvest falls short of hopes, Argentine farms are still aiming to increase production by more than 10 percent to 50 million tonnes.
Output of wheat, the season's first major crop, may jump from a bit over nine million tonnes last season to 14 million tonnes or more. Wheat exports would more than double.
Consultant Daniel Miro said a bumper harvest may cause transport and storage bottlenecks, delays and higher costs.
"Suppose we get a 14.5-million tonne wheat crop, this means we need to export 9.5 million tonnes," he said.

"Let's say that in December, January and February, you export a total of 6.5 million tonnes. But at the end of February the corn starts, the sunflower starts, and you still have about 3 million tonnes of wheat sitting there to be exported."
Miro recently told Argentine farm industry members that fees for transport and storage could rise as high as $20 a tonne.

"Transport and storage costs could rise. The final element is what will be the attitude of the farmer. Will he want to price a lot of wheat in December and January, price his corn in March?," he said.
He added, "If everyone wants to price his grain in December and January, then you'll have significant discounts."

He said farmers' sales to exporters are actually considerably behind last season, with only about 400,000 tonnes sold. "You have to add about 1 million tonnes priced through the futures and options market. But adding all that up, you only have about 10 percent of the crop with any sort of pricing."
But Agriculture Secretariat advisor Patricio Lamarca said that fears of a harvest bottlenecks are exaggerated.

"The thing is that the people are making their proyections on the basis of what happened in the past; 1984 was a disaster, there were piles of grain all over the place exposed to the weather," he said.

But Lamarca, who is secretary to a joint private and public commission established last year to plot the future of Argentina's grains business, said that much investment had since been made in transport and storage capacity.

A commission study recently estimated Argentina's total grains storage capacity at 46 million tonnes. While this is well below the optimum levels of probably 120 to 130 percent harvest output, today's capacity should just be about able to cope with this season's likely crop, Lamarca said.

"We are aware that there could be problems in some areas, but these should be compensated in other zones. In the southeast of Buenos Aires there is a serious storage deficit, but you have to consider also that today's storage facilities are much more efficient than in the past," he said.
He said that importers of storage equipment were working to capicity and that the nation's truck fleet has been modernizing fast since 1992.
Investment will have to continue if Argentine harvests keep growing. Argentine government and producers hope the country will soon produce 60 million tonnes a year of grains.
